title: The Three Christs of Ypsilanti Experiment
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover the Three Christs of Ypsilanti experiment, a 1950s-60s social psychology study by Milton Rokeach, who gathered three male patients at Ypsilanti State Hospital in Michigan who each claimed to be Jesus Christ, hoping confrontation would shatter their delusions. Covers Rokeach's identity-belief theory and the "belief that you are who you are" anecdote about calling his daughters by each other's names, the Voltaire story of Simone Morin, the three men's backgrounds (Joseph Cassel, Clyde Benson, Leon/Rex), the failed confrontation phase, Rokeach's later use of fake letters from authority figures (Madam Yeti Woman, Dr. Yoder, the archangel Michael's stand-in) and placebo pills, the ethical criticism, Rokeach's later regret and 1981 reissue, and his later self-confrontation method. Also discusses the 2021 film The Three Christs and a listener mail about stepping on cracks symmetrically.

segments.title: Opening banter and film discussion
segments.summary: Hosts open with casual banter, then discuss their interest in the Three Christs of Ypsilanti study and the 2021 film about it, which they feel was over-sanitized.

segments.title: Milton Rokeach and the identity anecdote
segments.summary: Introduction of social psychologist Milton Rokeach, his belief-system theory, and the anecdote of calling his daughters by each other's names at dinner, which upset them. The hosts discuss how challenging identity can be traumatic.

segments.title: Origins of the idea and Voltaire's Simone Morin
segments.summary: Rokeach's plan to test identity challenges on institutionalized people with delusions, his quoted rationale from the book, and his inspiration from a Harper's article and Voltaire's account of Simone Morin, a deluded man who was briefly knocked out of his delusion by meeting another man claiming to be Christ.

segments.title: Ypsilanti and recruiting the three men
segments.summary: Background on Ypsilanti as a town and the asylum system, Michigan state hospitals with about twenty-five thousand patients, and how Rokeach found six self-declared Christs, three of whom were consistent, two at Ypsilanti. The men were given perks to participate.

segments.title: Profiles of Joseph, Clyde, and Leon
segments.summary: Biographies of the three men under pseudonyms: Joseph Cassel, who claimed to be God and had a difficult childhood and hoarding habits; Clyde Benson, a heavy drinker diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia who claimed to be Jesus; and Leon, a younger man whose mother had religious delusions and who claimed to be Jesus Christ.

segments.title: Confrontation phase and the men's truce
segments.summary: The three men initially dug in and reinforced their identities rather than being shaken. Each had his own explanation of the others, but they eventually developed a live-and-let-live truce. Graduate assistants grew uneasy, and Rokeach read them a hostile newspaper story, prompting Leon to push back.

segments.title: Letter-writing campaign with fake authority figures
segments.summary: Rokeach hired a young woman to flirt with Leon, then escalated by posing as authority figures from the men's delusions through letters: Madam Yeti Woman for Leon, Dr. Yoder for Joseph, and a fake uncle voice call. Leon's letters ended when he asked to stop. Joseph received placebo pills, and the letters were eventually abandoned.

segments.title: Criticism, Rokeach's regret, and later work
segments.summary: The study was published in 1964 and widely criticized. Rokeach later regretted it, wrote a new foreword in 1981, and died in 1988 after a thirteen-year battle with spinal cancer. He developed self-confrontation, a later method. The hosts compare the study to the Stanford prison experiment and criticize his self-focused regret.

segments.title: Listener mail: stepping on cracks
segments.summary: Listener Jared Miller writes about the urge to match sensations on each foot, such as stepping on cracks or tile edges, and the hosts share similar habits.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with an email address for listeners and the show's credits.
